questions.question: Which of the following religion is NOT originated in India?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following religion is NOT originated in India?
questions.solution:
Zoroastrianism, the ancient pre-Islamic religion of Iran.

Key Points

  • That survives there in isolated areas and, more prosperously, in India, where the descendants of Zoroastrian Iranian (Persian) immigrants are known as Parsis, or Parsees.
  • Buddhism, a religion that more than 300 million people currently practice, was founded in northeastern India by Prince Siddhartha in the sixth century B.C.
  • Sikhism was born in the Punjab area of South Asia, which now falls into the present-day states of India and Pakistan.
    • The main religions of the area at the time were Hinduism and Islam.
    • The Sikh faith began around 1500 CE when Guru Nanak began teaching a faith that was quite distinct from Hinduism and Islam.
  • Jainism originated in the 7th–5th century BCE in the Ganges basin of eastern India, the scene of intense religious speculation and activity at that time.
    •  This new religious perspective promoted asceticism, the abandonment of ritual, domestic and social action, and the attainment of spiritual illumination in an attempt to win, through one’s own efforts, freedom from repeated rebirth.

questions.question: Who defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the second battle of Tarain in 1192 AD?
questions.questionHtml: Who defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the second battle of Tarain in 1192 AD?
questions.solution: Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the second battle of Tarain in 1192 AD. The second battle of Tarain was fought between Prithviraj Chauhan and Muhammad Ghori in which Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated and captured by Muhammad Ghori. This battle marked the end of the Chauhan dynasty and the beginning of the Muslim rule in North India.

questions.question: The Great Stupa at Sanchi was built by ______.
questions.questionHtml: The Great Stupa at Sanchi was built by ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Ashoka.

Key Points

  • Sanchi is a Buddhist complex, famous for its Great Stupa, on a hilltop at Sanchi Town in Raisen District of the State of Madhya Pradesh, India.
  • The Great Stupa at Sanchi is one of the oldest stone structures in India and an important monument of Indian Architecture.
  • It was originally commissioned by the emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.
  • Its nucleus was a simple hemispherical brick structure built over the relics of the Buddha.

Additional Information

  • Ashoka is also known as Ashoka the Great, was an Indian emperor of the Maurya Dynasty, who ruled almost all of the Indian subcontinent from 268 to 232 BCE.
  • He was the grandson of the dynasty's founder Chandragupta Maurya.
  • Ashoka promoted the spread of Buddhism across ancient Asia.

questions.question: Svetambara and Digambara are two sects of the _______ community.
questions.questionHtml: Svetambara and Digambara are two sects of the _______ community.
questions.solution:
• Svetambara and Digambara are two sects of the Jain community.
  • Svetambara Jains are “those who wear white” and is one of the two important sects of Jainism.
  • Svetambaras unlike Digambaras do not believe in renunciation of clothes for attaining liberation.
  • They also believe that anybody can attain liberation(including women).
  • Digamabara Jains are those to whom “space is the garment” and do not wear anything.
  • The Digambara Jains worship completely nude idols of tirthankaras (omniscient beings) and siddha (liberated souls). The tirthankara is represented either seated in yoga posture or standing in the Kayotsarga posture.
  • They believe that liberation can only be attained through male body and nudity is necessary to break the bondage of illusory world.
  • Extra:-
    •   Jainsim has 24 teerthankaras (those who have conquered the illusory world and cycles of birth and death and those who lead others towards liberation)
    • Rishabnath was the first Jain teerthankar and the founder of Jainism.
    • Mahavira was the last and 24th Jain teerthankar.
    • Five main vows of Jainism:-
  • ahiṃsā (non-violence), satya (truth), asteya (not stealing), brahmacharya (celibacy or chastity or sexual continence), and aparigraha (non-attachment)

  • Vishakhadatta was an Indian Sanskrit poet and playwright. 
  • He wrote political drama Mudraraksasa.

questions.question: The first battle of Tarain was fought between ___________.
questions.questionHtml: The first battle of Tarain was fought between ___________.

options.text: Prithviraj Chauhan and Mohammad Bin Qasim
options.html: Prithviraj Chauhan and Mohammad Bin Qasim

questions.solution: The first battle of Tarain was fought in 1191 CE near Thanesar, present-day Haryana, between Prithviraj Chauhan, the king of Ajmer and Delhi, and Muhammad Ghori, the ruler of the Ghurids in Afghanistan. The battle was over the control of the northwestern regions of India. Mohammad Bin Qasim, Mahmud Ghaznavi, and Qutubuddin Aibak did not participate in this battle. Mohammad Bin Qasim invaded Sindh in 712 CE, Mahmud Ghaznavi invaded India in the 11th century, and Qutubuddin Aibak, a later figure, became the first Sultan of Delhi after Ghori's death.

questions.question: In which of the following states was Lord Mahavira born?
questions.questionHtml: In which of the following states was Lord Mahavira born?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Bihar.

Key Points

  • Mahavira, also known as Vardhamana, born in the Vajji Kingdom, identical to modern-day Vaishali in Bihar.
  • Lord Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism who succeeded the 23ed Tirthankara, Parshvanatha.
  • According to Jain texts, Lord Mahavira was born on the 13th day of the bright half of the moon in the month of Chaitra.
  • Mahavira was born in King Siddhartha of Kundagrama and Queen Trishala, a Lichchhavi princess in the year 540 BC.
  • Mahavira belongs to the Ikshvaku dynasty.
  • He died at the age of 72 in 468 BCE in Pavapuri in Bihar.

questions.question: Where was the capital of Gandhara, one of the sixteen Mahajanpadas?
questions.questionHtml: Where was the capital of Gandhara, one of the sixteen Mahajanpadas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Takshashila 

  • Gandhara was an ancient kingdom situated along the Kabul and Swat rivers of Afghanistan and Pakistan.
  • The capital of Gandhara was Takshashila also known as Taxila.
  • 16 kingdoms were included in Mahajanapadas.
  • Ancient Buddhist Literature, Anguttara Nikaya text gives the list 16 Mahajanapadas.
  • They are - Kashi, Kosala, Anga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Machcha, Surasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja.
  • These Mahajanpadas are either Monarchy or a Republics (Ganasanghas).
  • The important Republics of this period were the Sakyas of Kapilavastu and the Licchavis of Vaishali.
  • The important monarchical Mahajanpadas of this period were Kaushambi (Vatsa), Magadha, Kosala, and Avanti.

questions.question: When was the 2 nd battle of Tarain fought?
questions.questionHtml: When was the 2<sup>nd</sup> battle of Tarain fought?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1192.

Key Points

  • The 2nd Battle of Tarain in 1192 AD, was fought between Prithviraj Chauhan and Muhammad Ghori.
    • It led to Prithviraj’s defeat and capture by Muhammad Ghori.
  • Prithviraja III, a member of the Chauhan (Chahamana) dynasty, was a king of Sapadalaksha, with his capital located at Ajmer, Rajasthan.
    • He was also referred to as Prithviraj Chauhan or Rai Pithora. Prithviraj, who ascended to the throne as a minor in 1177 CE, inherited a kingdom that spanned from Thanesar in the north to Jahazpur (Mewar) in the south.
    • He was born into the Chahamana dynasty in the year 1166 AD, in what is now modern-day Rajasthan, India.
    • He sought to expand this realm through military campaigns against neighboring kingdoms, chiefly the Chandelas.
    • In 1191 AD, Prithviraj and Ghori clashed in the First Battle of Tarain, where Prithviraj achieved a significant victory.
    • The tides turned in the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 AD, leading to Prithviraj’s defeat and capture by Muhammad Ghori. This marked the end of Prithviraj Chauhan’s rule.

questions.question: In the context of ancient Indian culture, the words/names 'nagara', 'vesara' and 'Dravidian' are associated with:
questions.questionHtml: In the context of ancient Indian culture, the words/names 'nagara', 'vesara' and 'Dravidian' are associated with:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Temple architectural stylesKey Points

  • Different styles of temple architecture have been built in different parts of India since ancient times.
  • Due to geographical, ethnic and historical diversity, different types of temples have been built in different parts of the country.
  • Temple architecture in North India is called Nagara, while temple architecture in South India is called Dravidian style of temple architecture.
  • The Vesara style of temple architecture is a combination of Nagara and Dravidian architectural styles.
  • Vesara is also an independent temple architectural style.
  • The city style temples are found in stone platforms.
  • There are no gates in city-style temples.

questions.question: Which two kings fought in the Battle of Hydaspes?
questions.questionHtml: Which two kings fought in the Battle of Hydaspes?
questions.solution:
• In 326 BC, Alexander the Great faced King Porus in the Battle of the Hydaspes, also known as the Battle of Jhelum.
  • It took place on the banks of the Jhelum River (called as Hydaspes by the ancient Greeks) in the Punjab area of India (modern-day Punjab, Pakistan).
  • The conflict ended with a Greek triumph and Porus' capitulation.
  • Large swaths of Punjab were integrated into the Alexandrian Empire, and Alexander reinstalled the vanquished and dethroned Porus as a subordinate ruler.
  • One of Alexander's "masterpieces" was his choice to cross the monsoon-swollen river despite intense Indian monitoring in order to catch Porus' army off-guard.

    • Abhidhamma Pitaka: It was composed at the third council which was held under Ashoka at Patliputra.

questions.question: Which of the following varnas was responsible for protecting people and administering justice in ancient India as per rules laid down by the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following varnas was responsible for protecting people and administering justice in ancient India as per rules laid down by the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras?
questions.solution:
• The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras also contained rules about the ideal “occupations” of the four categories or varnas.
  • Brahmanas were supposed to study and teach the Vedas, perform sacrifices and get sacrifices performed, and give and receive gifts.
  • Kshatriyas were to engage in warfare, protect people and administer justice, study the Vedas, get sacrifices performed, and make gifts.
  • The last three “occupations” were also assigned to the Vaishyas, who were in addition expected to engage in agriculture, pastoralism and trade.
  • Shudras were assigned only one occupation – that of serving the three “higher” varnas.
  • The Brahmanas evolved two or three strategies for enforcing these norms. One, as we have just seen, was to assert that the varna order was of divine origin.
  • Second, they advised kings to ensure that these norms were followed within their kingdoms.
  • And third, they attempted to persuade people that their status was determined by birth. However, this was not always easy. So prescriptions were often reinforced by stories told in the Mahabharata and other texts.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is "Third Buddhist Council – Pataliputra".

Important Points

  • Six Buddhist Councils marked important turning points in the story of early Buddhism.
  • This story spans the time from immediately after the death and Parinirvana of the historical Buddha in the 5th century BCE to sometime early in the first millennium CE.
  • This is also the story of sectarian clashes and the eventual Great Schism that resulted in the two major schools, Theravada and Mahayana.
  • In total, 6 Buddhist councils were convened.

The description of the six Buddhist councils has been given below:

First Buddhist Council :

  • It was held soon after the Mahaparinirvan of the Buddha, around 483 BC under the patronage of King Ajatshatru.
  • It was presided by Mahakasyapa, a monk. The council was held in the Sattapani cave at Rajgriha.
  • The council was held with the purpose of preserving Buddha’s teachings (Sutta) and rules for disciples. During this council, the teachings of Buddha were divided into three Pitakas.
  • The significance of the First Council is that 500 senior monks adopted the Vinaya-Pitaka and Sutta-Pitaka as the accurate teaching of the Buddha, to be remembered and kept by generations of nuns and monks to come.

 

Second Buddhist Council :

  • The Second Buddhist Council was held at Vaisali (or Vaishali), an ancient city in what is now the state of Bihar in northern India, bordering Nepal under the patronage of King Kalasoka while it was presided by Sabakami.
  • This Council probably was held about a century after the first one, or about 383 BCE.
  • It was called to discuss monastic practices, in particular, whether monks could be allowed to handle money.

 

Third Buddhist Council :

  • It was held in 250 BC at Pataliputra under the patronage of King Asoka.
  • It was presided by Moggliputta Tissa. The third part of the Tripitaka was coded in the Pali language.
  • This Council appears to have met to compose commentaries on the Tipitaka.

 

Fourth Buddhist Council :

  • The fourth Buddhist council was held in 72 AD at Kundalvana, Kashmir.
  • It was presided by Vasumitra, while Asvaghosa was his deputy.
  • The council was held under the patronage of Kushan King Kanishka of the Kushan Empire.
  • Buddhism was divided into two sects namely Mahayana and Hinayana.

 

Fifth Buddhist Council :

  • The fifth Buddhist council was held in Mandalay, Burma in the year 1871 under the patronage of King Mindon.
  • It was presided by Jagarabhivamsa, Narindhabhidhaja and Sumangalasami.
  • During this council, 729 stone slabs were engraved with Buddhist teachings.

 

Sixth Buddhist Council :

  • The Sixth Buddhist Council was held in 1954 in Burma at Kaba Aye, Yangoon.
  • It was held under the patronage of the Burmese government and it was presided by Prime Minister U Nu.
  • The council commemorated 2500 years of Buddhism.

questions.question: Who among the following was a Gupta ruler?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following was a Gupta ruler?
questions.solution:
• Vikramaditya(Chandra Gupta-II) was a Gupta ruler.
  • He was one of the Gupta Empire's most powerful Emperors in northern India.
  • He vanquished the Western Kshatrapas and spread the Gupta empire from the Indus River in the west to the eastern Bengal region, and from the northern Himalayan foothills to the southern Narmada River.
  • During the rule of Chandragupta II, the Gupta Empire reached its zenith.
  • He was the dynasty's second ruler to bear the name "Chandragupta" , the first being his grandfather Chandragupta I.

questions.question: Who among the following is the author of the epic poem ‘Ramcharitmanas’?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following is the author of the epic poem ‘Ramcharitmanas’?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is "Tulsidas".

Important Points

  • Tulsidas, the author of Ramcharitmanas was born in Rajpur in the Banda district of Uttar Pradesh in the 16th century.
  • Tulsidas is considered to be an incarnation of Valmiki, the sage who composed the original Ramayana and is counted among the foremost devotees of Lord Rama.
  • He was devoted to Rama.
  • Tulsidas was a devotee of Lord Rama from early childhood, and these words affected him deeply.
  • He left his home a family to become a wandering mendicant in search of the abiding love of his Lord Rama.
  • He is also the author of several other works including Vinaya Patrika, Gitavali, Dohavali, and Kavitavali.
  • His minor works include Baravai Ramayana, Janaki Mangal, Ramalala Nahachhu, Ramajna Prashna, Parvati Mangal, Krishna Gitavali, Hanuman Bahuka, Sankata Mochana and Vairagya Sandipini.
  • Furthermore, he is the seer of the Hanuman Chalisa, a powerful and popular mantra for Hanuman, in 40 verses.

Additional Information

  • Ramcharitmanas is an epic poem in Awadhi language, composed with the aid of using the 16th-century Indian bhakti poet Goswami Tulsidas.
  • The phrase Ramcharitmanas actually means "Lake of the deeds of Rama".
  • It is taken into consideration as one of the finest works of Hindi literature.
  • The paintings have variously been acclaimed as "the dwelling sum of Indian culture", "the tallest tree withinside the magic lawn of medieval Indian poetry", "the finest ebook of all devotional literature" and "the first-rate and maximum sincere manual to the famous dwelling religion of the Indian people".

questions.question: The Harappan site of Dholavira is located in which of the following states?
questions.questionHtml: The Harappan site of Dholavira is located in which of the following states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is ​Gujarat.

Key Points

  • The Harappan site of Dholavira is located in Gujarat.
  • In the great ran of Kutch of Gujarat, at Bhachau taluka, Dholavira is a village.
  • On Khadir Island, the site is located.

questions.question: Which Turkish invader attacked and raided the temple of Somnath in 1025 AD?
questions.questionHtml: Which Turkish invader attacked and raided the temple of Somnath in 1025 AD?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Mahmud Ghazni.

Key Points

  • Turkish invader Mahmud Ghazni, attacked and raided the temple of Somnath in 1025 AD.
  • The first of India's twelve sacred jyotirlingas is said to have arisen at the elaborately carved honey-colored Somnath temple or Deo Patan, is located in Prabhas Patan, Veraval in Gujarat, India.
    • It is said that Shiva manifested there as a blazing column of light.
    • The temples are situated where the Sarasvati, Hiran, and Kapila rivers converge, and the shoreline where they are built is touched by the ebb and flow of the Arabian Sea.
    • Although the timeline of the ancient temple starts in 649 BC, it is thought to be older.
    • Though it's difficult to see them through the foggy glass, vibrant dioramas depicting the Shiva narrative border the north side of the temple grounds.
    • The temple was reconstructed several times in the past after repeated destruction by multiple Muslim invaders and rulers, notably starting with an attack by Mahmud Ghazni in the 11th century.
      • The Pran-Pratistha at the existing temple was done on 11th May 1951 by then President of India, Dr. Rajendra Prasad.

Additional Information

  • Muhammad Yamin ad-Dawlah In the province of Ghazna, Mahmud ibn Sebuktigin was born on November 2, 971.
    • He founded the Turkic Ghaznavid dynasty, which ruled from 998 to 1030.
    • By the time of his death, his domain had grown into a vast military empire that included Khwarazm in Transoxiana, Punjab in India, Makran, and northwest Iran itself.
    • Famous Poet Patronized by Mahmud Ghazni were Firdausi who wrote Shahnameh and Alberuni who wrote Kitab-i-hind.
    • Mahmud invaded Gujarat in 1025, plundering the Somnath shrine and destroying its jyotirlinga. His loot included 2 million dinars. Somnath was conquered, and Anhilwara was invaded as retaliation.
  • Mu'izz ad-Din Muhammad, also called Muhammad of Ghor, ruled the Ghurid Empire as its lone ruler from 1202 to 1206, having served as its sultan from 1173 to 1202.
    • He is credited with bringing about centuries-long Muslim hegemony on the Indian subcontinent.
    • Originating from Persia, Muhammad Ghori reigned over portions of what is now Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Iran, Pakistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan.
  • Muhammad bin Tughluq (MBT) was the son of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, also known as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, who founded the Tughlaq dynasty by subduing the Delhi Sultanate. 
    • Other names for him are Ulugh Khan and Prince Fakhr Malik Jauna Khan.
    • The Deccan region of India, which is now Maharashtra, is home to Daulatabad, also called Devagiri, and it was Tughluq who ordered the relocation of his capital from Delhi.
    • He introduced token money in the form of brass and copper coins with a par value with gold and silver coins.

questions.question: Which of the following Buddhist texts is based on the conversation between the Buddhist sage Nagasena and Indo Greek king Menander?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following Buddhist texts is based on the conversation between the Buddhist sage Nagasena and Indo Greek king Menander?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Milindapanha.

Key Points

  • Milindapanha
    • An important Buddhist text that records the dialogue between the Indo-Greek King Menander (Milinda) and the Buddhist sage Nagasena.
    • It focuses on philosophical discussions and does not mention Pushyamitra Shunga or his Ashvamedha sacrifice.

Additional Information

  •  Mahavamsa
    • It is a poem written in the Pali language. It consists of information about the spread of Buddhism.
    • It was written during the reign of King Vijaya.
  • Dhammapada
    • The first discovery of the Prakrit text of the Dhammapada in Kharosthi was made in 1892 by the French traveller Dutreuil de Hhins, he also founded altogether three fragments in Khotan, which lie despatched to Paris.
    • The Dhammapada is the only text of which a fragment has been preserved in Kharosthi, a script in which two recensions of Asoka's Rock Edicts, at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, are inscribed, and this is the only Buddhist text which has been hitherto found composed in a Prakrit dialect.
    • The manuscript is one of the earliest finds from Khotan.
    • Among later finds in Khotan, we have to mention a few documents containing dispositions and reports of local authorities, instructions, regulations, official and private correspondence — all inscribed in the Kharosthi script and drawn up in a Prakrit dialect.
    • "Dhammapada," is a compound term composed of dhamma and pada.
    • Dhamma refers to the Buddha's "doctrine" and Pada means "foot".
  • Prajnaparamita
    • Prajnaparamita Sutras and Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra are Mahayana Buddhist texts.
    • The Prajnaparamita Sutras focus on the concept of 'perfection of wisdom' or 'prajna'.
    • The Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra discusses profound aspects of Buddhist philosophy with a lay disciple as the protagonist.

questions.question: The kingdoms of Chola, Chera and Pandyas belong to which period in the ancient India?
questions.questionHtml: The kingdoms of Chola, Chera and Pandyas belong to which period in the ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Sangam Period.

Key Points

  • The Sangam Age, sometimes referred to as the Tamil Sangam period, was an important period in South India's history. It is generally believed that the Sangam era occurred between 300 BCE and 300 CE.
  • Three dynasties—the Chera, Chola, and Pandyas—ruled the Tamil nation during the Sangam Period. They were Muvendar, jointly as well.
  • For administrative convenience, the kingdom was split into the following divisions: Mandalam (territory), Nadu (province), Ur (town), Perur (large village), and Sirur (small village).
  • More terms used in sangam age:
    • Karai: Land tax 
    • Ulgu: Customs duties
    • Iravu: Forced gift/extra demand 
    • Irai: Tribute paid by feudatories 
    • Variyar: Tax collector
    • Vanigar: Traders and Merchants
    • Arasar: Ruling Class
    • Vellalars: Dominant Agricultural caste
    • Uzhavars: Middle-class Agricultural caste

Additional Information

  • Mauryan Period:

    • Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Mauryan Empire.
    • He is referred to in Greek sources as Sandrokottos.
    • In 321 BC, he defeated Dhana Nanda and took the throne with the aid of a politically astute and clever Brahmin named Kautilya.
    • Megasthenes served as the Greek representative in the court of Chandragupta.
    • He led an expansionist policy that subjugated nearly all of modern-day India, except a few isolated areas in the far south and Kalinga.
    • Bindusara is the second Mauryan Empire ruler.
    • 297–273 BC was his rule period.
    • He was also called Amitraghata (Slayer of foes).
    • Ashoka mentions in his inscription that he conquered Kalinga after becoming the king for eight years.
    • Kalinga was a region located in present-day Odisha and parts of Andhra Pradesh.
    • Ashoka established Ujjain and Takshashila (later Taxila) as the regional capitals of his kingdom.
  • Mahajanapada period:
    • ​In Jambudipa (Bharatvarsha), there were sixteen republics of significant size and authority known as "Solasa Mahajanapada," according to the Buddhist canonical scripture Anguttara Nikaya.
    • The sixteen Mahajanapadas belonged to either a republican or monarchical political structure.
    • The republics were located in present-day Punjab in northwest India and along the foothills of the Himalayas, while the monarchies were primarily located in the Gangetic Plains.
    • They existed from the 6th to 4th century BCE.
    • The Anguttara Nikaya lists sixteen Mahajanapadas, and they are:
    • Mahajanpada Capital Present Location
      Anga Champa Munger and Bhagalpur(Bihar)
      Magadha Girivraja| Rajagriha Gaya and Patna(Bihar)
      Kasi Kasi Banaras(UP)
      Vatsa Kausambi Allahabad(UP)
      Kosala Sravasti Eastern Uttar Pradesh
      Saurasena Mathura Western Uttar Pradesh
      Panchala Ahichchatra and Kampliya Western Uttar Pradesh
      Kuru Indraprastha Meerut(UP) and Southeastern Haryana
      Matsya Viratnagar Jaipur(Rajasthan)
      Chedi Sothivati Jaipur(Rajasthan)
      Avanti Ujjaini or Mahismati Malwa (Madhya Pradesh)
      Gandhara Taxila Rawalpindi(Pakistan)
      Kamboja Pooncha Rajori and Hajra(Kashmir)
      Ashmaka or Assaka Pratisthan/ Paithan Bank of Godavari(Andhra Pradesh)
      Vajji Vaishali Bihar
      Malla Kusinara Deoria and Uttar Pradesh

questions.question: Who among the following was greatest ruler of Pratihara Dynasty?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following was greatest ruler of Pratihara Dynasty?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Mihir Bhoja​.

Key Points

  • Mihir Bhoja was the greatest ruler of the Pratihara Dynasty.
  • The Pratiharas or the Gurjar Pratiharas rose to power after the fall of the Pushyabuti Dynasty.
  • There are major two lineages of Pratihara known that was founded by Harichandra and Nagabhatta.
  • The line of Harichandra (6th -9th century AD) ruled over Marwar in Rajasthan and that of Nagabhatta I (8th - 11th century AD) ruled over Ujjain and Kannauj.
  • Bhoja or Mihir Bhoja was the greatest ruler of this dynasty.

Additional Information

Ruler His rule

  • Was succeeded by Mihir Bhoja.

  • Laid the foundation of Pratihara rule at Ujjain.

Samantasena

questions.question: Which of the following was the last invasion by Mahmud Ghazni outside Punjab?

Additional Information

  • Somnath temple:

      • It is said that Shiva manifested there as a blazing column of light.
      • The temples are situated where the Sarasvati, Hiran, and Kapila rivers converge, and the shoreline where they are built is touched by the ebb and flow of the Arabian Sea.
      • Although the timeline of the ancient temple starts in 649 BC, it is thought to be older.
      • Though it's difficult to see them through the foggy glass, vibrant dioramas depicting the Shiva narrative border the north side of the temple grounds.
      • The temple was reconstructed several times in the past after repeated destruction by multiple Muslim invaders and rulers, notably starting with an attack by Mahmud Ghazni in the 11th century.
        • The Pran-Pratistha at the existing temple was done on May 11, 1951, by the then President of India, Dr. Rajendra Prasad.

questions.question: Rulers belonging to Gurjara - Pratihara, Rashtrakuta and Pala dynasties fought for control over _____.
questions.questionHtml: Rulers belonging to Gurjara - Pratihara, Rashtrakuta and Pala dynasties fought for control over _____.

The Gurjara-Pratihara, Rashtrakuta, and Pala dynasties fought for its control due to its significance in trade and politics during that era.

questions.question: Which king inscribed the Hathigumpha (Elephant Cave) inscription in Udayagiri Hills, Odisha?
questions.questionHtml: Which king inscribed the Hathigumpha (Elephant Cave) inscription in Udayagiri Hills, Odisha?
questions.solution:
• Kharavela, the then Emperor of Kalinga,  inscribed the Hathigumpha (Elephant Cave) inscription in Udayagiri Hills, Odisha during 2nd century BCE.
  • The Hathigumpha inscription situated near Bhubaneswar gives information about year-wise achievements of Kharavela.
  • The inscription starts with a version of the auspicious Jain Namokar Mantra.
  • The Inscription consists of seventeen lines in deep-cut Brahmi script.
  • The contents of the Hatigumpha Inscriptions are taken as true records of Kharavela’s reign.
  • The inscription gives a note on the political, religious, cultural and social condition of Kalinga during that glorious period.

questions.question: Ravikirti was a court poet of which Chalukya ruler?
questions.questionHtml: Ravikirti was a court poet of which Chalukya ruler?
questions.solution: Ravikirti was the court poet of Pulakeshin II, the best-known Chalukyan king. Ravikirti composed a prashasti in praise of Pulakeshin II and mentioned his expeditions along both the west and the east coasts. Pulakeshin II also attacked the Pallava king who took shelter behind the walls of Kanchipuram. Thus, option 2 is the correct answer.

questions.question: While Magadha was a powerful Mahajanapada, Vajji, with its capital at Vaishali (Bihar), was under a different form of government known as:
questions.questionHtml: While Magadha was a powerful Mahajanapada, Vajji, with its capital at Vaishali (Bihar), was under a different form of government known as:
questions.solution:
• While Magadha was a powerful Mahajanapada, Vajji, with its capital at Vaishali (Bihar), was under a different form of government known as Gana or Sangha.
  • A gana or sangha had not one, but many rulers.
  • Even if there were thousands of men who ruled, they were still called as Raja.
  • All of them performed the rituals together and also met for assemblies.

questions.question: Which of the following city was the capital of the Pandyas?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following city was the capital of the Pandyas?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Madurai.

Key Points

  • The Pandyas were one of the ancient Tamil dynasties that ruled over parts of southern India from around the 6th century BCE to the 17th century CE.
    • Their kingdom was centered in what is now Tamil Nadu.
  • They belonged to the group of three ancient Sangam age kingdoms known as "Muvendar," or the three crowns- The Pandyas, Chera and Chola.
  • Under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan, the Pandyas entered their golden age, expanding their empire into Telugu country and invading Sri Lanka to conquer the northern half of the island.
  • They ruled initially from Korkai, a seaport on the Indian peninsula's southernmost tip, and later shifted to Madurai.
  • Madurai was one of the major cities in the Pandya kingdom and was the capital for many centuries.
    • It was known for its impressive architecture, including the Meenakshi Amman Temple and the Thirumalai Nayak Palace.

Additional Information

  • Kallupatti and Kariapatti are both small towns in Tamil Nadu that have historical significance but were not major centers of power during the Pandya era.
  • Palamedu is a village in Tamil Nadu that is known for its annual bull-taming festival.
  • The territory of the Pandyas is known as Pandymandalam, Thenmandalam, or Pandianadu.
    • The region known as Pandy Mandalam or Pandy Nadu was split up into numerous valanadus, which were then further separated into numerous kurrams and nadus (meaning group of villages).
    • Royal authorities were referred to by different titles:
      • The Prime Minister was called Uttaramantri.
      • The name of the royal secretariat was Eluttu Mandapam.
      • The titles of the military leaders were Palli Velan, Parantakan Pallivelan, Maran Adittan, and Tennavan Tamizhavel.6
  • The political distribution of land was as follows:
    • Brahmins were given land in Salabogam.
    • The land allotted to ironsmiths was known as Tattarkani.
    • The area belonging to the Carpenters was called Taccu-maniyam.
    • The land provided to the Brahmin community for educational reasons was known as Bhattavriutti.
  • Early Tamilakam coins featured the Three Crowned Kings, a tiger, a fish, and a bow, which represented the Cholas, Pandyas, and Cheras respectively.
    • "Kodandaraman" and "Kanchi Valangum Perumal" were the names given to the Pandya coins with fish images.
  • The Pandyas are thought to have followed Jainism at first before switching to Shaivism.

questions.question: Where was the first Jain Mahasabha held?
questions.questionHtml: Where was the first Jain Mahasabha held?
questions.solution:
• The first Jain Mahasabha was held at Pataliputra(now known as Patna).
  • It was held in the beginning of the 3rd century BC by Sthulabahu.
  • The second councils were held simultaneously at Mathura and Vallabhi and the third at Vallabhi.
  • The Jain councils are associated with the revision and improvement of their sacred text termed as Jain Agamas.

questions.question: King Kharavela, the ancient Indian king whose biography is found in the famous Hathigumpha inscription, ruled from:
questions.questionHtml: King Kharavela, the ancient Indian king whose biography is found in the famous Hathigumpha inscription, ruled from:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Kalinga.

  • King Kharavela, the ancient Indian king whose biography is found in the famous Hathigumpha inscription, ruled in Kalinga, Odisha.
  • In the second century BCE, the region was ruled by him.

Key Points

  • He belonged to Maha-Meghavahana dynasty.
  • This dynasty is also known as the Chedi dynasty.
  • Vriddharaja was his predecessor.
  • He belonged to Jainism.

Important Points

  • The hathigumpha inscription is the rock-cut inscription.
  • The inscription is the basic source of kharvela king.
  • The inscription is interpreted differently by different scholars.
  • The military victories, patronage of arts, welfare activities and repair work are mentioned by the inscription.
  • But the achievement of the king is exaggerated by the inscription.
